turns.speaker: A
turns.text: When indie developers decide how to charge for an app, the big question is often subscription or lifetime purchase. Which do you prefer?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: It depends on the app. A subscription model gives you regular income every month. That's great if your app has ongoing costs, like servers, or if you keep adding new content.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: But many users don't like subscriptions.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: That's true. People talk about subscription fatigue. They already pay for music, video and cloud storage, so they're careful about adding another monthly fee, especially for a simple tool.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: So a lifetime purchase is more user-friendly?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: For some apps, yes. Users pay once and own it forever. They feel respected. But for the developer, the income stops unless new people keep buying.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: How do you compare the two?

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: A useful idea is customer lifetime value. That's the total money one user brings you over the whole time they use your app. A small subscription for three years might bring more than one lifetime purchase. Or it might not, if people cancel quickly.

turns.speaker: B
turns.text: Many developers do. They offer a monthly plan, a yearly plan and a higher one-time price for lifetime access. Users choose what feels right, and you learn a lot from what they pick.
